LAPSED GIFTS AND THE ANTI-LAPSE STATUTE (PROB. CODE §§ 21109-21111; IN RE TUNG TRUST; ESTATE OF STOCKIRD) — INFORMATION SHEET
Prepared for Ya-Ching Tung · revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011

PURPOSE OF THIS ANTI-LAPSE STATUTE INFORMATION SHEET
This information sheet describes California's rules on what happens when a beneficiary named in a will, trust, or other at-death transfer instrument dies before the person making the transfer — the default rule that the gift "lapses" (fails), the anti-lapse statute that substitutes the deceased beneficiary's issue in the beneficiary's place when the beneficiary was kindred of the transferor or of the transferor's spouse and the instrument expresses no contrary intention, and the rules that direct where a gift goes when it fails and no substitute gift applies — as background in connection with the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung, the gift under that instrument to Lin-Chuan Yeh (son of Ya-Ching Tung), Lin-Chuan Yeh's death on July 26, 2016, Ya-Ching Tung's later death on May 7, 2019, and a petition by Nicholas Yeh concerning the disposition of that gift. This document covers the statutory survival requirement and its clear-and-convincing-evidence rule, the statute's application to wills, trusts, and other instruments alike, the substitute gift to a deceased transferee's issue and its extension to class gifts, the "kindred" limitation on who qualifies as a transferee, the instrument's power to displace the statute by a contrary intention or a survival requirement and the 2026 Court of Appeal decision distinguishing a survival requirement from a clause that merely defines who is deemed to have predeceased the settlor, the interpretive rules courts apply in deciding whether a contrary intention appears, the statutory order of destinations for a failed gift, the rule that a failed share of a residuary gift left to several people passes to the other residuary beneficiaries, and the Court of Appeal's holding that the kindred limitation does not narrow that residuary rule. Every clause states what the statutes and published decisions provide; none states how those authorities apply to Ya-Ching Tung's instrument or to Lin-Chuan Yeh's gift.

THE DEFAULT RULE: A TRANSFEREE WHO DOES NOT SURVIVE THE TRANSFEROR TAKES NOTHING (PROB. CODE § 21109)
The starting point is Probate Code section 21109. Under subdivision (a), a transferee who fails to survive the transferor of an at-death transfer — or who fails to survive until any later time the instrument itself requires — does not take under the instrument. Subdivision (b) supplies the rule of proof for an instrument-imposed survival period: if it cannot be determined by clear and convincing evidence that the transferee survived until the required future time, the transferee is deemed not to have survived it. The Court of Appeal's 2026 decision in In re Tung Trust summarizes the same default in a single sentence: as a general matter, when the recipient of a trust benefit fails to survive the transferor of an at-death transfer, the transfer fails. The same opinion observes that the 120-hour survival rules the Legislature has enacted for intestate succession and for the California statutory will have no counterpart for trusts and non-statutory wills; for those instruments, section 21109 governs unless the anti-lapse statute applies. As applied to the instrument of Ya-Ching Tung, section 21109 is the rule that would cause the gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh, who died on July 26, 2016 before Ya-Ching Tung's death on May 7, 2019, to fail unless a substitute gift or other provision of law preserves it.

THE RULES APPLY TO WILLS, TRUSTS, AND OTHER INSTRUMENTS ALIKE, AND THE TRANSFEROR'S EXPRESSED INTENTION CONTROLS (PROB. CODE §§ 21101, 21102)
Sections 21109 through 21111 sit in Part 1 of Division 11 of the Probate Code, the rules for interpretation of instruments. Section 21101 provides that, unless the provision or context otherwise requires, that part applies to a will, trust, deed, and any other instrument. Section 21102 states the governing principle for the whole part: the intention of the transferor as expressed in the instrument controls the legal effect of the dispositions made in the instrument; the statutory rules of construction apply only where the instrument does not indicate the transferor's intention; and nothing in the section limits the use of extrinsic evidence, to the extent otherwise authorized by law, to determine that intention. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust, applying these provisions to a revocable living trust, stated flatly that the anti-lapse statute applies in the same manner to wills and trusts. The revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung is therefore within the class of instruments to which sections 21109 through 21111 apply, and the controlling question under section 21102 is what that instrument itself expresses.

THE ANTI-LAPSE STATUTE'S SUBSTITUTE GIFT: THE DECEASED TRANSFEREE'S ISSUE TAKE IN THE TRANSFEREE'S PLACE (PROB. CODE § 21110(A))
Section 21110, subdivision (a), is California's anti-lapse statute. Subject to subdivision (b), if a transferee is dead when the instrument is executed, or fails or is treated as failing to survive the transferor (or a future time the instrument requires), the issue of the deceased transferee take in the transferee's place in the manner provided in section 240 — the representation formula under which the property is divided into equal shares at the nearest generation of the transferee's issue that has living members, with a deceased member's share divided among that member's own issue. The subdivision extends the substitute gift to a member of a class gift, unless the class member's death occurred before the instrument was executed and the transferor knew that fact when executing it. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust explained the statute's function: it prevents the unintended disinheritance of descendants of a transferee by creating a presumption that the transferor intended the descendants to receive the transfer in place of a transferee who has died by the time of the transfer, and, quoting Estate of Mooney, it is called an "antilapse" statute because the devises it protects would otherwise lapse and pass by intestacy. Where the statute applies to the gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh under the instrument of Ya-Ching Tung, the persons who would take in Lin-Chuan Yeh's place are Lin-Chuan Yeh's issue, in the shares section 240 prescribes.

WHO COUNTS AS A "TRANSFEREE": KINDRED OF THE TRANSFEROR OR OF THE TRANSFEROR'S SPOUSE, BUT NEVER THE SPOUSE (PROB. CODE § 21110(C))
The substitute gift is available only for a limited class of beneficiaries. Section 21110, subdivision (c), defines "transferee," as used in the anti-lapse statute, as a person who is kindred of the transferor or kindred of a surviving, deceased, or former spouse of the transferor — and expressly excludes a spouse of the transferor. The Court of Appeal in Estate of Stockird, citing the Law Revision Commission's comment, explained that "kindred" refers to persons related by blood, and other persons listed in section 21115 (the Probate Code's rules on halfbloods, adoptees, and similar relationships). In Stockird, the testator's holographic will left 35 percent of everything to an aunt who had been married to the testator's uncle but was not related to the testator by blood; the aunt predeceased the testator. It was undisputed that the aunt was not kindred, so section 21110 did not apply and her issue were not entitled to her share under the anti-lapse statute — the same conclusion the trial court, both parties, and the Court of Appeal all reached before turning to the separate question of where the failed share went. Whether Lin-Chuan Yeh, identified in this sheet as son of Ya-Ching Tung, falls within subdivision (c) determines whether the substitute gift in subdivision (a) is available at all.

DISPLACING THE STATUTE: A CONTRARY INTENTION, A SUBSTITUTE DISPOSITION, OR A SURVIVAL REQUIREMENT (PROB. CODE § 21110(B))
The anti-lapse statute is a default rule that yields to the instrument. Section 21110, subdivision (b), provides that the issue of a deceased transferee do not take in the transferee's place if the instrument expresses a contrary intention or a substitute disposition, and it then identifies two provisions that constitute a contrary intention as a matter of law: a requirement that the initial transferee survive the transferor or survive for a specified period of time after the transferor's death, and a requirement that the initial transferee survive until a future time related to the probate of the transferor's will or the administration of the transferor's estate. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust restated the long-settled judicial gloss, quoting Estate of Salisbury: the California anti-lapse statute will not be applied where the testator has expressed, with sufficient clarity, a contrary intention, but if no contrary intent appears the statute must be read into the will; the paramount question is whether such intent is plainly indicated or shown with a reasonable degree of certainty. Tung also described the survival clause held sufficient in Burkett v. Capovilla — a trust provision stating that for all gifts under the instrument the beneficiary must survive for sixty days before entitlement to such gifts — as a survival requirement under subdivision (b) that expressed an intention contrary to the anti-lapse statute. Whether the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung contains a survival requirement, a substitute disposition, or other language of contrary intention is therefore the pivot on which the substitute gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh's issue turns.

A CLAUSE THAT ONLY DEFINES WHO IS "DEEMED TO HAVE PREDECEASED" THE SETTLOR IS NOT A SURVIVAL REQUIREMENT — IN RE TUNG TRUST (2026)
In re Tung Trust, decided by the Second District Court of Appeal on June 9, 2026 and certified for publication, is the first published California decision to examine what language does and does not amount to a survival requirement under section 21110, subdivision (b). Ya-Ching Tung's 2011 revocable trust left all real property to her son Lin-Chuan, who died in 2016, nearly three years before Tung; Lin-Chuan left three children. The trust's "miscellaneous provisions" included a paragraph titled "Survivor by 30 Days" stating that if any person named in the trust failed to survive a settlor for thirty days, then for all purposes of the trust the person would be considered to have predeceased the settlor. The probate court treated that clause as a survival requirement, found a contrary intention, and ruled that the gift to Lin-Chuan lapsed. The Court of Appeal reversed. It held that, on its face, the clause was not a requirement that the initial transferee survive the transferor or survive for a specified period in order for the issue to receive the gift: it did not state, explicitly or implicitly, that a gift was conditioned on the beneficiary surviving the settlor, but merely established circumstances in which a beneficiary who survived the settlor would nonetheless be deemed to have predeceased her. The court contrasted the Burkett provision, which expressly addressed gifts and used mandatory survival language — the Tung trust did neither. The court added that if Tung had intended the transfer to fail if Lin-Chuan predeceased her, she could simply have modified the dispositive paragraph to say the property went to him unless he did not survive her. Because the trust contained no survival requirement under subdivision (b) and did not otherwise evidence a contrary intention, the anti-lapse statute applied and Lin-Chuan's transfer passed to his children. Tung thus draws a line between a clause imposing a condition of survival on a gift and a clause that merely defines the order of deaths, and that distinction is directly relevant to any survivorship-related language in the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung.

HOW COURTS DECIDE WHETHER A CONTRARY INTENTION APPEARS: THE WHOLE INSTRUMENT, THE PREFERENCE AGAINST INTESTACY, AND THE TRANSFEROR'S PRESUMED KNOWLEDGE OF THE STATUTE
In re Tung Trust also lays out the interpretive method a court uses in deciding whether an instrument expresses a contrary intention. The inquiry is not confined to the disputed clause standing alone; the court must determine whether the instrument, viewed holistically in light of that clause, expressed a contrary intention. This document covers the statutory survival requirement and its clear-and-convincing-evidence rule, the statute's application to wills, trusts, and other instruments alike, the substitute gift to a deceased transferee's issue and its extension to class gifts, the "kindred" limitation on who qualifies as a transferee, the instrument's power to displace the statute by a contrary intention or a survival requirement and the 2026 Court of Appeal decision distinguishing a survival requirement from a clause that merely defines who is deemed to have predeceased the settlor, the interpretive rules courts apply in deciding whether a contrary intention appears, the statutory order of destinations for a failed gift, the rule that a failed share of a residuary gift left to several people passes to the other residuary beneficiaries, and the Court of Appeal's holding that the kindred limitation does not narrow that residuary rule. The starting point is Probate Code section 21109. Under subdivision (a), a transferee who fails to survive the transferor of an at-death transfer — or who fails to survive until any later time the instrument itself requires — does not take under the instrument. Subdivision (b) supplies the rule of proof for an instrument-imposed survival period: if it cannot be determined by clear and convincing evidence that the transferee survived until the required future time, the transferee is deemed not to have survived it. The Court of Appeal's 2026 decision in In re Tung Trust summarizes the same default in a single sentence: as a general matter, when the recipient of a trust benefit fails to survive the transferor of an at-death transfer, the transfer fails. The same opinion observes that the 120-hour survival rules the Legislature has enacted for intestate succession and for the California statutory will have no counterpart for trusts and non-statutory wills; for those instruments, section 21109 governs unless the anti-lapse statute applies. Section 21101 provides that, unless the provision or context otherwise requires, that part applies to a will, trust, deed, and any other instrument. Section 21102 states the governing principle for the whole part: the intention of the transferor as expressed in the instrument controls the legal effect of the dispositions made in the instrument; the statutory rules of construction apply only where the instrument does not indicate the transferor's intention; and nothing in the section limits the use of extrinsic evidence, to the extent otherwise authorized by law, to determine that intention. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust, applying these provisions to a revocable living trust, stated flatly that the anti-lapse statute applies in the same manner to wills and trusts. The revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung is therefore within the class of instruments to which sections 21109 through 21111 apply, and the controlling question under section 21102 is what that instrument itself expresses.

Subject to subdivision (b), if a transferee is dead when the instrument is executed, or fails or is treated as failing to survive the transferor (or a future time the instrument requires), the issue of the deceased transferee take in the transferee's place in the manner provided in section 240 — the representation formula under which the property is divided into equal shares at the nearest generation of the transferee's issue that has living members, with a deceased member's share divided among that member's own issue. The subdivision extends the substitute gift to a member of a class gift, unless the class member's death occurred before the instrument was executed and the transferor knew that fact when executing it. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust explained the statute's function: it prevents the unintended disinheritance of descendants of a transferee by creating a presumption that the transferor intended the descendants to receive the transfer in place of a transferee who has died by the time of the transfer, and, quoting Estate of Mooney, it is called an "antilapse" statute because the devises it protects would otherwise lapse and pass by intestacy. Where the statute applies to the gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh under the instrument of Ya-Ching Tung, the persons who would take in Lin-Chuan Yeh's place are Lin-Chuan Yeh's issue, in the shares section 240 prescribes.

Section 21110, subdivision (b), provides that the issue of a deceased transferee do not take in the transferee's place if the instrument expresses a contrary intention or a substitute disposition, and it then identifies two provisions that constitute a contrary intention as a matter of law: a requirement that the initial transferee survive the transferor or survive for a specified period of time after the transferor's death, and a requirement that the initial transferee survive until a future time related to the probate of the transferor's will or the administration of the transferor's estate. The Court of Appeal in In re Tung Trust restated the long-settled judicial gloss, quoting Estate of Salisbury: the California anti-lapse statute will not be applied where the testator has expressed, with sufficient clarity, a contrary intention, but if no contrary intent appears the statute must be read into the will; the paramount question is whether such intent is plainly indicated or shown with a reasonable degree of certainty. Tung also described the survival clause held sufficient in Burkett v. Capovilla — a trust provision stating that for all gifts under the instrument the beneficiary must survive for sixty days before entitlement to such gifts — as a survival requirement under subdivision (b) that expressed an intention contrary to the anti-lapse statute. expectedJSON.body: In re Tung Trust, decided by the Second District Court of Appeal on June 9, 2026 and certified for publication, is the first published California decision to examine what language does and does not amount to a survival requirement under section 21110, subdivision (b). Ya-Ching Tung's 2011 revocable trust left all real property to her son Lin-Chuan, who died in 2016, nearly three years before Tung; Lin-Chuan left three children. The trust's "miscellaneous provisions" included a paragraph titled "Survivor by 30 Days" stating that if any person named in the trust failed to survive a settlor for thirty days, then for all purposes of the trust the person would be considered to have predeceased the settlor. The probate court treated that clause as a survival requirement, found a contrary intention, and ruled that the gift to Lin-Chuan lapsed. The Court of Appeal reversed. It held that, on its face, the clause was not a requirement that the initial transferee survive the transferor or survive for a specified period in order for the issue to receive the gift: it did not state, explicitly or implicitly, that a gift was conditioned on the beneficiary surviving the settlor, but merely established circumstances in which a beneficiary who survived the settlor would nonetheless be deemed to have predeceased her. The court contrasted the Burkett provision, which expressly addressed gifts and used mandatory survival language — the Tung trust did neither. The court added that if Tung had intended the transfer to fail if Lin-Chuan predeceased her, she could simply have modified the dispositive paragraph to say the property went to him unless he did not survive her. Because the trust contained no survival requirement under subdivision (b) and did not otherwise evidence a contrary intention, the anti-lapse statute applied and Lin-Chuan's transfer passed to his children. Tung thus draws a line between a clause imposing a condition of survival on a gift and a clause that merely defines the order of deaths, and that distinction is directly relevant to any survivorship-related language in the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung.

expectedJSON.body: In re Tung Trust also lays out the interpretive method a court uses in deciding whether an instrument expresses a contrary intention. The inquiry is not confined to the disputed clause standing alone; the court must determine whether the instrument, viewed holistically in light of that clause, expressed a contrary intention. The Court of Appeal applied the Probate Code's rules of construction: all parts of an instrument are construed in relation to each other so as, if possible, to form a consistent whole (section 21121), and preference is given to an interpretation that will prevent intestacy or failure of a transfer rather than one that will result in intestacy or failure of a transfer (section 21120). In Tung, other provisions of the trust — an "additions" clause directing property to a beneficiary's then-living issue if the beneficiary was not living, and a no-contest clause treating a contestant as having predeceased the settlor "without surviving issue" — indicated that the settlor did not intend to exclude a deceased child's children. The court also invoked the rule, quoted from Estate of Salisbury, that a testator is presumed to know the law at the time of making the will, and reasoned that the settlor must be assumed to have understood the anti-lapse statute when she established the trust, so that it was unreasonable to infer she had included a boilerplate survivor clause to disinherit her grandchildren in a highly oblique manner. The court reviewed the trust de novo because the case turned on the instrument's terms without conflicting extrinsic evidence, and it did not reach the grandchildren's extrinsic-evidence arguments. These are the tools a court would bring to the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung in deciding whether any of its provisions displaces the substitute gift to the issue of Lin-Chuan Yeh.

expectedJSON.body: When a gift fails and the anti-lapse statute does not preserve it, section 21111 supplies the destination. Subdivision (a), which operates subject to section 21110, provides that if a transfer fails for any reason the property passes (1) according to any alternative disposition the instrument itself provides for the event of failure; (2) if there is no alternative disposition but the instrument provides for the transfer of a residue, into the residue transferred under the instrument; and (3) if the instrument provides neither an alternative disposition nor a residue, or if the failed transfer is itself a residuary gift, to the decedent's estate. Subdivision (c) adds that a transfer of "all my estate" or words of similar import is a residuary gift for purposes of the section — a rule the Court of Appeal in Estate of Stockird applied to a holographic will leaving "all my property and everything I may be entitled to inherit," finding those words reflected an intent to give all of the testator's estate. Subdivision (d) directs that if the failure of a future interest results in an intestacy, the property passes to the transferor's heirs determined under section 21114. In In re Tung Trust the court noted that, without the anti-lapse statute, a specific gift of real property in a trust with no alternative disposition and no residuary clause would have reverted to the settlor's estate and apparently passed by intestacy. Under this framework, the destination of the gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh — if it fails — depends on whether the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung contains an alternative disposition, a residuary clause, or neither, and on whether the failed gift is itself residuary.

expectedJSON.body: Section 21111, subdivision (b), addresses the specific case of a residuary gift (or a future interest) transferred to two or more persons where the share of one transferee fails. Subject to section 21110, and where no alternative disposition is provided, the failed share passes to the other transferees in proportion to their other interest in the residuary gift or future interest. The Court of Appeal in Estate of Stockird held that this subdivision applies to every residuary co-beneficiary, not only to beneficiaries who are kindred of the transferor. There, the failed 35 percent residuary share belonged to an aunt by marriage who was not kindred, and the probate court had reasoned that the kindred definition of "transferee" in section 21110(c) carried over to section 21111(b), so that the failed share passed by intestacy to the testator's half brother rather than to the surviving residuary beneficiary, the testator's life partner. The Court of Appeal reversed. It held that section 21110(c) defines "transferee" only "as used in this section," that the Probate Code's general definition of transferee — a beneficiary, donee, or other recipient of an interest transferred by an instrument (section 81.5) — governs section 21111(b), and that this reading is confirmed by the Law Revision Commission's comments, which describe the 2002 amendment as abolishing the common-law "no residue of a residue" rule under which a lapsed share of the residue passed to the heirs at law. The court quoted the Commission's summary that a failed specific gift passes by intestacy absent an alternate or residuary disposition, while a failed residuary gift passes to the remaining residuary beneficiaries proportionately, and it grounded the result in the general principle that intestacy is to be avoided when possible. It directed that the failed share pass to the surviving residuary beneficiary, subject to a separately pending petition by the aunt's descendants to reform the will. If the gift to Lin-Chuan Yeh under the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung is a share of a residuary gift made to several persons, subdivision (b) as construed in Stockird is the rule that would govern the failed share whenever the substitute gift under section 21110 is unavailable.

expectedJSON.body: A related rule of construction in the same chapter governs a common form of alternative disposition. Section 21112 provides that a condition in a transfer of a present or future interest that refers to a person's death "with" or "without" issue, or to a person's "having" or "leaving" issue or no issue, or a condition based on words of similar import, is construed to refer to that person's being dead at the time the transfer takes effect in enjoyment and to the person either having or not having, as the case may be, issue who are alive at that time. Like the rest of Part 1 of Division 11, section 21112 applies to wills, trusts, and other instruments and yields to a contrary intention expressed in the instrument (sections 21101, 21102). If the revocable living trust dated October 24, 2011 of Ya-Ching Tung conditions a gift, or an alternative gift, on whether Lin-Chuan Yeh died with or without issue, section 21112 is the statutory rule for reading that condition.
